title: How often does a short window of sound sync real phones and cameras to within a video frame, and can a confidence set in one room hold in another?
lede: research programme: audio sync of free-running cameras and phones on real devices; step 1 on five real smartphones in a 200 ms and an 800 ms room (LibriWASN): clocks differ by up to 19 ppm, and with -10 dB of white noise GCC-PHAT misses a frame on 17-34% of 2 s windows against 5-7% for partial whitening; step 2a: Ianniello's threshold model, fed with each window's spectra, predicts the miss rate on real speech within a factor of 2 in 80% of 171 cells (running low), raw-bin PHAT misses more than its smoothed form (40% vs 33%), and with real babble noise PHAT becomes the best weighting, not the worst; step 2b, on the real phones: the same model is refuted (within x2 in 41 of 94 cells), right for 0.5 s windows but overpredicting misses by up to x5 at 2-4 s; step 3: a Learn-then-Test confidence gate set for 1% wrong among accepted windows holds across rooms and phones on average (1.45% and 0.57% for 2 s windows) but not across noise levels: calibrated without -10 dB audio it lets 4.7-7.3% wrong windows through, while requiring PHAT and partial whitening to agree cuts that to 1.4-2.6%; step 3b: gating per bin of a blind SNR estimate and refusing windows below the calibration range keeps the 1% bound under every shift (0.27% wrong at -10 dB room to room, keeping 74%), but under an unseen noise level it does so by refusing 93-99% of windows; using the threshold theory as the score does not transfer (2.3-5.4%)
summary: An open research programme (track 13, capture) on syncing free-running cameras and phones from their own sound: how often a short window fixes the offset to within one 30 fps frame on real devices, rooms and clocks, and whether a confidence calibrated in one room or rig keeps its failure rate in another. Step 1 (2026-11-13) runs on LibriWASN (Schmalenstroeer, Gburrek and Haeb-Umbach 2023; Zenodo, CC BY 4.0): five smartphones (Nexus, Pixel 6a, two Pixel 6, Pixel 7, Xiaomi) recording the same loudspeaker playback of LibriSpeech, 10 ten-minute sessions in a room with about 200 ms and 10 in one with about 800 ms of reverberation. Only the phone channels are fetched, by HTTP range requests, and none is committed. For each of the 200 phone pairs a reference line (20 s GCC windows every 10 s, Theil-Sen) is checked without ground truth: every pair kept at least 97% of its windows within 5 ms of the line, and the three lines of every phone triple add up to within 1.8 ms (median 0.3 to 0.5 ms), far under the 33 ms frame. The phones' sampling clocks differ by up to 19.1 ppm (median 13.7 ppm), the same within about 1 ppm from session to session and room to room. Short windows (0.5 to 4 s, 40 seeded times per pair and session, a simulated start-offset prior of ±1 s because the published files are pre-aligned) were scored for five weightings, with the recordings as published and with independent white noise added at 0 and −10 dB. With added noise, PHAT is the worst weighting in both real rooms and partial whitening (gamma 0.25 to 0) the best: at −10 dB, 2 s windows fail 16.9% and 33.6% of the time with PHAT against 5.0% and 7.2% with gamma 0.25 (95% session-bootstrap intervals separate), which reverses capture-reverbsync's finding in simulated rooms. The 800 ms room is harder than the 200 ms one at −10 dB, as predicted. As recorded, PHAT still fails 3.3% of 2 s windows in the 200 ms room (spread over all ten pairs at scattered wrong lags, cause open; gamma 0.25 removes nearly all of it) against a predicted under 1%. The peak-to-sidelobe ratio separates good from bad windows (AUROC 0.91 to 0.998 at 2 s), but a threshold set in one room to let at most 1% of accepted windows be wrong, applied in the other, holds on average over noise levels (0.6% to 1.6%) and not at −10 dB from the drier to the wetter room (3.7% for gamma 0.25, 5.5% for PHAT). Limits: one dataset, one loudspeaker playback of read speech, white rather than real noise, simulated start offsets, phones not cameras; the reference's own error (closure up to 1.8 ms) bounds sub-ms claims. Step 2a (2026-11-13) tests the threshold theory of time-delay estimation (H4). Ianniello's (1982) gross-error model is extended to weighted GCC (weight (GxxGyy)−γ/2), fed with each window's Welch spectra, and checked on 84,000 simulated windows: Gaussian signals, and real read speech (MS-SNSD, MIT) with white or real babble noise in dry rooms and statistical rooms of RT60 0.2 and 0.8 s. zenodo.org was unreachable from that session, so the LibriWASN check is step 2b, with its harness committed. On speech, the model predicts the share of windows more than a frame off within a factor of 2 in 137 of 171 scored cells (80%, against a pre-registered 75%). It runs low (median predicted/observed 0.58 to 0.74), misses most at 0 dB with 0.5 s windows, and agrees in 82 of 83 cells at −15 dB. The Gaussian check agreed in 32 of 36 cells, narrowly missing its pre-registered 90%. Step 1's GCC normalises each FFT bin by its own magnitude, and that costs PHAT: averaged over the speech cells it misses 39.7% against 32.6% for the same weighting from smoothed spectra. With real babble the weighting ranking flips: PHAT is best and plain correlation worst (0.8 s room, −10 dB, 2 s: 50% against 79%). Step 1's preference for partial whitening therefore holds for white noise only. As a blind confidence, the model's probability flags PHAT failures better than the peak-to-sidelobe ratio (median AUROC 0.85 against 0.74), but not for gamma 0.25. Limits: the rooms are statistical, the delays are simulated, the babble is independent per device rather than shared, and the H4 score uses spectra aligned at the true lag. Step 2b (2026-11-14) runs the same model window for window on the LibriWASN phones of step 1 (96,000 windows; the replay reproduced all 96 of step 1's miss rates exactly). H4 is refuted on real devices: the model is within a factor of 2 in 41 of 94 scored cells (44%, against the pre-registered 75%; Rice's variant 39/94). It now runs high (median predicted/observed 2.2, no cell underpredicted by more than x2), and its error grows with window length: 24 of 24 cells agree at 0.5 s, 1 of 24 at 2 s and 2 of 22 at 4 s, for every weighting. The 800 ms room agrees more often than the 200 ms one (52% against 35%), and raw-bin PHAT again misses more than smooth-weight PHAT at −10 dB (all 8 window-room cells). Why real recordings improve with window length faster than the theory says is open. Step 3 (2026-11-14) puts a distribution-free threshold on the peak-to-sidelobe ratio: Learn then Test (Angelopoulos et al. 2021), set for at most 1% wrong among accepted windows at delta 0.1, calibrated in one condition and tested in another on the same 96,000 windows. For 2 s windows with gamma 0.25, room to room gives 1.45% and 0.57% wrong among accepted (keeping 97 to 98%), and leaving each phone out gives 0.49% to 1.30%; but calibrating on the recordings as published and at 0 dB and testing at −10 dB gives 4.65% and 7.25%, because on cleaner audio the threshold falls to the floor. A gate calibrated on a mix of noise levels controls the mix, not the noisiest part. Requiring the PHAT and gamma 0.25 estimates to agree (post hoc) cuts the noise-shift failure to 1.43% and 2.57% at 2 s, though not at 1 s. Within one room 13% of session splits exceed 1% (the i.i.d. bound is 10%), because windows cluster by session. Two rooms, five phones and added white noise only. Step 3b (2026-11-14) tests two noise-aware gates on the same windows. A blind SNR estimate, the spread of a window’s 32 ms frame energies, separates the noise levels almost completely (2 s medians 21, 5.2 and 1.2 dB as recorded, at 0 dB and at −10 dB). Gating with one Learn-then-Test threshold per calibration quartile of that estimate, and refusing windows below the calibration’s range, keeps wrong-among-accepted under 1% in every shift: 0.27% room to room at −10 dB (keeping 74%, against 3.38% for the pooled gate), and 4% of within-room session splits above 1% (pooled 15%). Under the unseen noise level it lets nothing wrong through, by refusing 93% and 99% of windows, most of them right. Scoring windows with the threshold theory instead of PSR is a slightly better flag for PHAT (AUROC 0.987 against 0.977) but does not carry the bound (2.25% and 5.37% under the noise shift). The recipe: cover the noise range in calibration, gate per blind-SNR bin, refuse below it. Added white noise only.
